solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Creature, rabbit, briefly seen by River Dee, perhaps (10)

indicators.note: a word said briefly is cut short, so NATTER loses its last letter
to be seen by something is to be beside it, so the pieces sit next to each other

blocks.note: to rabbit (on) is British slang for to chatter, NATTER, here without its last letter
R is the map abbreviation for river
the comedian Jack Dee is one Dee, so his first name stands in

explanation.surface: A nature-watcher spots a rabbit darting past on the banks of the River Dee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River Dee' looks like one place, but the river is only R; this Dee is the British comedian Jack Dee.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the natterjack is a British toad, one kind of creature.

clue.text: Ancient Greeks worshipped her near landing-place reportedly (4)

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: nigh is an old word for near
a quay is a wharf where boats land, and it is pronounced 'key'
the two words run together as one two-syllable name

explanation.surface: Ancient worshippers visit a shrine down by the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: NIGH plus QUAY, spoken, gives NIKE; the harbour setting hides that the landing-place is only there for its sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: Nike was the Greek goddess of victory, worshipped across ancient Greece.

clue.text: Elevated shot, notice tennis players will use it (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the letters up means reading them from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: a nip is a small shot of spirits
to spot something is to notice it

explanation.surface: A tennis coach explains a lofted shot, pinning up a notice for the players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevated shot' looks like a lob on court, but 'shot' is a drink. 'Elevated' only works as a turnaround because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: topspin is the forward rotation tennis players put on the ball.

clue.text: Engineer, i.e. MSc, working as secret influential adviser (8,5)

indicators.note: letters that are working are being put to use and moved about, so they change order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters; 'i.e.' and 'MSc' are just their letters

explanation.surface: An engineer with a master's degree quietly steers the boss's decisions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' reads as a job title or a verb meaning to contrive, but it is only letters. The phrase is French for 'grey eminence', first used of Cardinal Richelieu's adviser.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowed phrase: an éminence grise is someone who wields power unofficially from behind the scenes.

clue.text: Day after rock star almost gets nicked (6)

indicators.note: almost the whole name, so it stops one letter short
D for day follows the shortened rock star in the answer

blocks.note: Mick Jagger of the Rolling Stones, without his final R
D is the standard abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A rock star is arrested the day after a gig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets nicked' is British slang for gets arrested, which the surface leans on; the definition uses 'nicked' in its other sense, notched.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in a second sense: an edge covered in small nicks is notched and uneven.

clue.text: Somewhere revel carousing around, keeping comparatively smart (8)

indicators.note: the words keep the answer inside them, running across their boundaries
the kept letters are turned around, so they are read right to left

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word, all of the second, and the first letter of the third, read from right to left

explanation.surface: Partygoers carouse somewhere, and one of them keeps a bit sharper than the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: somewhe(RE REVEL C)arousing, read backwards, gives C-LEVER-ERE. The run crosses three words, so reading forwards will not find it.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative adjective: 'smart' and 'clever' are synonyms, and 'comparatively' asks for the -er form.

clue.text: Taking coat from stylish young woman (4)

indicators.note: a coat is the outer layer, so taking it off strips the first and last letters

blocks.note: classy means stylish; lose the outer C and Y

explanation.surface: Someone helps a fashionable young woman off with her coat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the coat a garment; here it is the word's outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional synonym: lass is the Scottish and northern English word for a girl or young woman.

clue.text: Titular Shakespeare role, male last to die maybe (7)

indicators.note: 'last' places M at the very end, after the Shakespeare role

blocks.note: Mark Antony is named in the title of Antony and Cleopatra
M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: An actor playing Shakespeare's title hero is the last man to die on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last to die' reads as a death scene, but 'last' only places M, and 'die maybe' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: 'die' is the opposite of 'live', so it is one instance of an antonym.

clue.text: Boy racer, possibly amphetamine addict (10)

blocks.note: a boy racer is British slang for a young man who drives fast, flashy cars
'speed' is street slang for amphetamine

explanation.surface: A young tearaway driver turns out to be hooked on pills.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses share one phrase: an obsession with going fast, and a habit named after the drug's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are informal: one lives for fast driving, the other is dependent on the drug called speed.

clue.text: Writer, man Hislop regularly is cutting about (7)

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every second letter is taken
turned about, the chosen letters face the other way
the letters cut into the man, splitting him in two

blocks.note: a king is one of the men on a chessboard
h(I)s(L)o(P), the even letters

explanation.surface: The satirist Ian Hislop takes his pen to a rival writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' as a chess piece is a common crossword device. Ian Hislop edits the British satirical magazine Private Eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Rudyard Kipling, author of The Jungle Book, is one writer.

clue.text: Style improvement, it lengthened pockets (7)

indicators.note: to pocket something is to hold it inside, as these words hold the answer

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word, all of the second, and the first two of the third

explanation.surface: A tailor improves a jacket by lengthening its pockets.
explanation.walkthrough: improvem(ENT IT LE)ngthened. 'Style' sits at the start like a fashion word, but it is a verb: to style someone is to call them by a title.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to style someone 'Sir' is to give them that title.

clue.text: Slow, as in late to make latte, say? (4-9)

blocks.note: the surface pushes a barista running late with a coffee

blocks.clueFragment: as in late to make latte, say?
blocks.note: the setter means spelling: LATE must swallow a T, the abbreviation for time, to become LATTE

explanation.surface: A barista is running late with a coffee order.
explanation.walkthrough: A word that eats a T is, read literally, time-consuming, since T is short for time. That second reading backs up the plain definition 'Slow'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a time-consuming job takes a long time, so it is slow.

clue.text: Fixed earlier, printer deemed to be broken (13)

indicators.note: something broken falls apart, and its pieces can be put back in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: A printer that was repaired earlier is now declared broken again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' in the surface sounds like repaired; the definition uses its other sense, settled.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something predetermined was settled, fixed, in advance.

clue.text: Succeeded boarding ship mines damaged, creating mischief (10)

indicators.note: to board a ship is to go inside it, so S goes in among the other letters
damaged letters are knocked out of shape, into a new order

blocks.note: S for succeeded, as in lists of monarchs
anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A boarding party damages a ship's mines, causing havoc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boarding ship' looks like a naval raid; it only tells S to go inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: impishness is playful naughtiness, the spirit of mischief.

clue.text: Current champ tours Olympic city (6)

indicators.note: to tour a place is to travel all round it, so MUNCH goes round I

blocks.note: to champ is to chew noisily
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: The reigning champion takes a tour of a city that has hosted the Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current champ' reads as the title holder, but 'champ' is the verb to chew.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this German city hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.

clue.text: Former Wimbledon champion (not British) essentially encouraging novice (8)

indicators.note: the bracketed 'not British' tells us the B is left out
the essence of a word is its core, the middle letter

blocks.note: John Newcombe, the Australian who won Wimbledon three times, minus B for British
the sixth of eleven letters, the middle of encouRaging

explanation.surface: A retired Wimbledon champion from abroad encourages a beginner.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets read as an aside about his nationality, which is true of Newcombe, but they are the instruction to delete.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a newcomer is someone new to an activity, a novice.

clue.text: German condemned probing newspaper piece (8)

indicators.note: a condemned building is fit only to be pulled down, so the word's letters are rebuilt
a probe goes in, so the letters go into the newspaper

blocks.note: FT is the Financial Times
GERMAN rearranged

explanation.surface: A German journalist is condemned for a probing newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newspaper piece' looks like one phrase, an article, but 'piece' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fragment is a small piece broken off something.

clue.text: Obtain survey Neil oddly defends, rounding numbers (8)

indicators.note: oddly means in the odd positions: first, third, fifth letters
defenders surround what they protect, so these letters go round GET
to round is to turn back, so everything is read backwards

blocks.note: (S)u(R)v(E)y (N)e(I)l, the odd letters across both words
to get is to obtain

explanation.surface: Someone wants a survey that Neil defends by rounding off its figures.
explanation.walkthrough: SRE and NI go round GET, and the whole reads backwards. 'Rounding numbers' reads as arithmetic, but 'numbers' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: integers are whole numbers, one class of number.

clue.text: Expression about Harry’s weight (7)

indicators.note: about means around, so the expression wraps around the next word

blocks.note: tone of voice is a person's expression
to harry someone is to pester or nag them

explanation.surface: A comment is made about Prince Harry's weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a name but is the verb to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: tonnage is weight measured in tons, especially of ships or cargo.

clue.text: In the morning, energy drink will stop flipping problem (6)

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning
gin, the spirit
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A morning energy drink is supposed to put a stop to some nagging trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping problem' reads as a mild British curse, like 'blooming problem'; here 'flipping' turns the letters back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an enigma is a puzzle, a problem hard to solve.

clue.text: Choose KLM for flights and share costs equally (2,5)

blocks.note: KLM is the national airline of the Netherlands, so this reads literally as travelling the Dutch way
an idiom for everyone paying their own part of the bill

explanation.surface: Friends pick the Dutch airline for a trip and split the fares.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: 'go' is taken literally, flying with the Dutch airline.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom in both halves: to go Dutch is to split a bill, and literally to travel Dutch.

clue.text: Dumping married rock singer (6)

indicators.note: to dump something is to throw it out, so the M is removed

blocks.note: to rock is to shake or tremble
M for married, as on forms; it is taken out

explanation.surface: A rock singer ditches his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock singer' looks like one musician; 'rock' is the verb to shake.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: a treble is a boy who sings the highest part in a choir.

clue.text: Where one might shoot, which could suggest thin gun? (7-6)

blocks.note: the surface pushes a firing range and a flimsy weapon
the setter means a reverse clue: grind up the first word of the answer and you get the letters THIN GUN

explanation.surface: A shooter looks for a good spot, worried that the gun looks flimsy.
explanation.walkthrough: HUNTING is an anagram of THIN GUN, and 'ground' is a fair anagram signal, so the answer is itself an instruction that produces the clue's words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: a hunting ground is land where game is shot.

clue.text: Smirk of embarrassment when spilling tea (4)

indicators.note: spilt tea runs out of the cup, so CHA runs out of the word

blocks.note: chagrin is embarrassed annoyance
cha is British slang for tea, from Chinese; it is taken out

explanation.surface: Someone smirks awkwardly after knocking over the tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The embarrassment in the surface is the word being cut, not the reason for the smirk.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a smirk is a smug, knowing kind of smile.

clue.text: Stand before door that revolves (7)

indicators.note: something that revolves turns round, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: ere is an old word for before
a gate is an outdoor door

explanation.surface: Someone waits in front of a revolving door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' looks like a verb, as in standing at a door; it is the noun, a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist word from French: an étagère is a stand of open shelves for displaying ornaments.

clue.text: Attack famous surgeon behind back of pub (7)

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter
to stand behind something is to come after it, so the surgeon follows B

blocks.note: the last letter of pub
Joseph Lister, the British pioneer of antiseptic surgery

explanation.surface: A well-known surgeon is set upon behind a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attack' reads as a physical assault; the answer is the verb for scalding criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: to blister someone is to attack them with criticism harsh enough to burn.

clue.text: Drop something in the garden? (4)

blocks.note: a verb: trees let their leaves fall this way
a noun: the wooden hut where tools are kept

explanation.surface: A gardener lets something fall among the plants.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites reading the clue as one garden scene, with trees dropping leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: to cast off, as leaves or skin, and a small outbuilding.

clue.text: Support son facing awkward tenth green, one birdie ultimately missed (10)

indicators.note: to face something is to stand in front of it, so S comes first
awkward letters sit in an awkward, jumbled order
ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter of birdie is used
something missed is left out, so that E drops from the fodder

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
anagram fodder before one letter is removed
the last letter of birdie; one of the three Es in the fodder goes

explanation.surface: A golfer's son helps on a tricky tenth green after missing a birdie putt.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf words are misdirection: a birdie is one under par on a hole, but here it only supplies its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to support a wall or a case is to make it stronger.
